brief.question: How do Kirchenbauer et al.'s watermark and Christ et al.'s undetectable watermark each work, and what is needed to detect each one?

claims.text: Kirchenbauer et al.'s scheme is essentially the idea of using a {0,1}-valued hash function and sampling tokens with preference for those satisfying h(x_j)=1, so that watermarked text has more tokens hashing to 1 than to 0.
This biasing strategy significantly alters the output distribution and is easily detectable because it prefers half of the words in the token set.
Christ et al.'s watermark algorithm receives from the model a full description of the probability distribution p_i for each token.

Using this knowledge, the algorithm computes the empirical entropy of its output thus far and, once the empirical entropy is sufficiently high, uses the output as a random seed for a PRF used to embed the watermark in subsequent tokens.
The algorithm alters the output distribution only once it has collected enough entropy.
In one construction, the watermark distribution is defined as the distribution of x drawn from the model conditioned on O(x)=0^b, and detection simply checks whether O(x)=0^b.

In another construction, the secret key shared by the watermarked model and the detection algorithm is a sequence of uniformly chosen real numbers in [0,1], and from the perspective of a user who does not know the secret key the distribution of outputs is not changed at all.
In an undetectable scheme, the only thing kept secret from the distinguisher is the secret key.
A watermarking scheme can be made public by publishing the secret key, after which everyone can run the detection algorithm, but the scheme is no longer undetectable.

Undetectability is possible only against a computationally bounded adversary, since using a polynomial number of queries and exponential running time any nontrivial watermarking scheme can be detected.
Undetectability is impossible if outputs of low empirical entropy are watermarked, since such a watermark can be detected using exp(t) queries and time.

Liu et al. note that the consistent increase in response length in DeepSeek-R1-Zero is frequently interpreted as an indication of the development of advanced reasoning abilities such as self-reflection.
Liu et al. argue that the observed increase in response length may also be attributed to a bias inherent in the GRPO objective function.
Liu et al. identify an optimization bias in GRPO that artificially increases response length, especially for incorrect outputs, during training.
Liu et al. report that average response lengths increased substantially across all categories, including correct responses, but that incorrect responses were notably longer than correct responses.

Liu et al. hypothesize that the longer average length of incorrect responses is because more challenging questions generally require longer responses and incorrect responses are more likely to originate from harder questions.
